existing_inputs.label: Surface-adjusted player rating (Elo/serve-return)
existing_inputs.why: Sets the base probability: a surface-blended Elo gap converts to a win probability, and the surface weighting is what separates a clay specialist from a hard-court player with the same overall rating.

existing_inputs.label: Opponent-adjusted serve and return components
existing_inputs.why: Match odds are really the pair's point-win rates on serve and return; adjusting each player's raw rates for the quality of opponents faced shows how this specific pairing plays, which a single rating hides.

existing_inputs.label: Hold/break probabilities and game-level Markov model
existing_inputs.why: Converts point-level serve/return strength into game, set and match probability through the hold/break chain, so a small per-point edge is amplified in a best-of-five and diluted in a best-of-three.

existing_inputs.label: Match format (best-of-3/5, tiebreak, ad scoring)
existing_inputs.why: Best-of-five gives the stronger player more sets to express a per-point edge, so the same rating gap implies a more lopsided winner price than in best-of-three; the contract's format must be known before pricing.

existing_inputs.label: Fitness/injury/withdrawal and in-match retirement risk
existing_inputs.why: An injured or ill player wins less and may retire; the price moves only when the status is public, so the timestamp of the report matters more than the report itself.

existing_inputs.label: Fatigue (match length, back-to-back days, travel)
existing_inputs.why: Long previous matches, a short turnaround and late-night finishes lower serve speed and movement; the effect is largest in later rounds and best-of-five events.

existing_inputs.label: Court speed, altitude, balls, indoor/outdoor, weather
existing_inputs.why: Fast courts, altitude and indoor air raise hold rates and favour big servers, while slow clay favours returners and rallying; the effect scales with how different the two players' styles are.

existing_inputs.label: Head-to-head and style matchup
existing_inputs.why: Head-to-head only adds information once serve/return rates and handedness are controlled; a lopsided history with a small sample is mostly noise, but a stylistic mismatch (big server vs elite returner) persists.

existing_inputs.label: Rating uncertainty (returning, young, low-sample players)
existing_inputs.why: Returning, young and low-sample players have wide rating error; the winner price should be shrunk toward 50% less aggressively for them, and the market often over-trusts a single recent result.

existing_inputs.label: Retirement/walkover/suspension settlement wording
existing_inputs.why: Whether a retirement or walkover settles the winner contract as a win, void or loss changes which side is worth buying when one player is hurt; the exact contract wording decides the payoff.

existing_inputs.label: Closing bookmaker odds
existing_inputs.why: The sportsbook closing line is the efficient-market benchmark; any model must beat it, not just predict outcomes, and its timestamp vs the Kalshi quote determines whether the comparison is fair.

existing_inputs.label: De-vig method and favourite-longshot bias in tennis lines
existing_inputs.why: Choosing how to remove the book's margin (proportional, power, Shin) changes the implied probability of longshots by a few points; favourite-longshot bias in tennis lines is exactly where a mispricing study would look.

existing_inputs.label: Serve/return point-win probabilities by surface
existing_inputs.why: Raw serve-point and return-point win rates by surface are the building blocks of the pair model; their sample size per surface (few grass matches) limits how far they can be trusted.

existing_inputs.label: Recent form and match-load
existing_inputs.why: Recent results relative to rating expectation capture slumps and hot streaks only if they exceed what rating updates already absorb; most apparent form is regression to the rating.

existing_inputs.label: Second-serve and return vulnerability
existing_inputs.why: Break chances come mostly from second-serve points; a player with a weak second serve against a strong returner loses more games than their first-serve numbers imply.

existing_inputs.label: Cross-surface skill transfer and sample pooling
existing_inputs.why: Lets a player's thin clay or grass record borrow information from similar surfaces, which matters most early in the season and for players switching surface.

existing_inputs.label: Handedness and left-hander matchup
existing_inputs.why: A left-hander's serve patterns and ad-court slice are unusual to face, and the opponent's lack of practice against them shows in break rates, but the edge is small and shrinks with sample size.

existing_inputs.label: Travel and time-zone shift
existing_inputs.why: Long-haul travel and time shifts affect the first days of an event; it matters for early rounds after intercontinental swings and is largely gone by the quarterfinals.

existing_inputs.label: Rain suspension and postponement risk
existing_inputs.why: Rain delays and overnight suspensions change momentum, order of play and rest, and can leave a match unfinished past the contract's settlement window.

existing_interactions.hypothesis: Edge amplification in best-of-five means the same rating gap yields larger win probability.
Match-winner wording typically settles on the progression winner; injury risk changes both performance and the retirement path.
Serve dominance gets more weight on fast event conditions.
Heavy favourites against uncertain-rated opponents are where de-vig bias and rating noise interact most.

match_winner.existing_mechanism: Match-win probability is a function of the serve/return point-win edge on the actual surface, amplified by the number of sets, adjusted for fitness, fatigue and conditions, and tied to settlement rules for retirements. Elo by surface gives a robust base; opponent-adjusted serve/return gives pair-specific hold/break; the market's sharp close is the benchmark.
match_winner.label: Match winner

existing_inputs.label: Hold/break probabilities and game-level Markov model
existing_inputs.why: The game margin is the sum of break differentials over sets; a player who breaks more and holds more wins by larger margins, and the hold/break chain converts that into a spread distribution.

existing_inputs.label: Opponent-adjusted serve and return components
existing_inputs.why: Spread cover depends on the specific pair's break rates, so opponent-adjusted components replace each player's raw averages.

existing_inputs.label: Surface-adjusted player rating (Elo/serve-return)
existing_inputs.why: The rating gap sets the expected margin; the mapping from Elo gap to expected game margin is roughly linear in the middle and flattens at the extremes.

existing_inputs.label: Bagel/breadstick and lopsided-set propensity
existing_inputs.why: Fat tails in the margin come from 6-0 and 6-1 sets; players with high lopsided-set rates cover large handicaps more often than a normal approximation says.

existing_inputs.label: Within-match dependence and momentum
existing_inputs.why: Sets are not independent: a player who wins the first set tends to win the second, so margins have a heavier spread than independent-set models give.

existing_inputs.label: Match format (best-of-3/5, tiebreak, ad scoring)
existing_inputs.why: A handicap of -4.5 games means very different things in best-of-three and best-of-five; the set count and final-set rule set how large margins can get.

existing_inputs.label: Tour/gender and level differences
existing_inputs.why: WTA matches have more breaks and smaller expected margins than ATP for the same rating gap, so ATP-calibrated models mis-size women's spreads.

existing_inputs.label: Retirement and walkover base rates
existing_inputs.why: A mid-match retirement leaves a partial margin that usually settles the favourite's cover as lost or void.

existing_inputs.label: Retirement/walkover/suspension settlement wording
existing_inputs.why: Whether a retired match settles the spread on games played, as a win for the other player, or as void changes the value of the cover side.

existing_inputs.label: Cross-rung consistency of the threshold ladder
existing_inputs.why: Spread rungs must be monotone and consistent with the winner price; violations indicate stale quotes rather than mispricing.

existing_inputs.label: Second-serve and return vulnerability
existing_inputs.why: Game margins widen against a player with a weak second serve because they lose a higher share of their service games.

existing_inputs.label: Cross-surface skill transfer and sample pooling
existing_inputs.why: Pooling across surfaces stabilises margin estimates for players with few matches on the current surface.

existing_inputs.label: Fatigue (match length, back-to-back days, travel)
existing_inputs.why: Tired players lose more games late in matches, so fatigue widens margins in the final set more than it changes the winner.

existing_interactions.hypothesis: Game-differential tails come from lopsided sets, whose frequency exceeds iid predictions.
A retiring favourite leads in games but loses the match; settlement rules determine whether the spread counts.
Higher WTA break rates make spreads less sensitive to hold probability and more to return.

set_and_game_spreads.existing_mechanism: Spreads depend on the distribution of the game (or set) differential, not just the win probability: it needs the hold/break probabilities of both players, the match format and the lopsidedness distribution. Push rules and half-point lines matter. Ladders of spread lines must be consistent with the match-winner market and with each other.
set_and_game_spreads.label: Set and game spreads

existing_inputs.label: Hold/break probabilities and game-level Markov model
existing_inputs.why: Total games per set is driven by hold probabilities: two big servers hold often, push sets to 6-6 and raise totals, two weak servers trade breaks and shorten sets less predictably.

existing_inputs.label: Surface-adjusted player rating (Elo/serve-return)
existing_inputs.why: A large rating gap means more 6-2/6-1 sets and fewer games; a closeness measure from the surface rating gap is the main driver of the total ladder relative to the line.

existing_inputs.label: Match format (best-of-3/5, tiebreak, ad scoring)
existing_inputs.why: Best-of-five adds up to two sets and a larger total mechanically; the strike level should be read against the format's maximum and median game counts.

existing_inputs.label: Final-set rule and tiebreak format
existing_inputs.why: A final-set tiebreak versus advantage set changes the right tail of total games enormously (an advantage set can run to 20+ games), so it must match the event's rules.

existing_inputs.label: Probability a set reaches 6-6
existing_inputs.why: Each set that reaches 6-6 adds at least one game and often lifts the total over a strike; the probability depends on both players' hold rates.

existing_inputs.label: Bagel/breadstick and lopsided-set propensity
existing_inputs.why: Some players produce bagels and breadsticks often; a high lopsided-set rate pulls totals under and is partly independent of the average rating gap.

existing_inputs.label: Event-specific court speed history
existing_inputs.why: Courts at a given event play consistently fast or slow; the event's past hold percentage is a stronger predictor of games per set than the generic surface label.

existing_inputs.label: Retirement and walkover base rates
existing_inputs.why: A retirement truncates a match and usually settles totals as under or void; the base rate (higher in best-of-five and for injured players) sets how much under-risk the over carries.

existing_inputs.label: Retirement/walkover/suspension settlement wording
existing_inputs.why: Whether a retired match counts games played, voids, or settles on a minimum set count changes the value of the over side.

existing_inputs.label: Cross-rung consistency of the threshold ladder
existing_inputs.why: Totals are listed at several strikes at once; the ladder must be monotonic in probability, so crossed or flat rungs flag stale quotes rather than information.

existing_inputs.label: Serve/return point-win probabilities by surface
existing_inputs.why: Serve and return point rates by surface feed the game-level Markov model that generates the distribution of games per set.

existing_inputs.label: Tiebreak win rate and hold-under-pressure
existing_inputs.why: Tiebreak outcomes do not change the games count past 13 but do change set winners and match length; a player's tiebreak record is a weak, noisy trait.

existing_inputs.label: Start times, order of play, delays
existing_inputs.why: Night sessions, a delayed start or a roof closing change conditions; indoor conditions raise hold rates and totals.

existing_inputs.label: Historical realized frequency by strike/rung
existing_inputs.why: Historical realised frequency by games/sets rung shows where the ladder is systematically over- or under-priced before any player model is applied.

existing_inputs.label: Rally-length and return style profile
existing_inputs.why: Strong returners create breaks, shortening sets; rallying styles lengthen them.

existing_inputs.label: Expected number of service games/points
existing_inputs.why: Expected service games per set sets the games count.

existing_inputs.label: 1st-serve in%, 1st/2nd-serve points won by surface
existing_inputs.why: First-serve effectiveness drives hold rates.

existing_inputs.label: Break-point conversion/save luck regression
existing_inputs.why: Break-point conversion beyond expectation regresses.

existing_interactions.hypothesis: Two strong holders raise totals via both long sets and tiebreaks.
Heavy favourites in bo5 produce short sweeps; evenly matched pairs go long.
Retirement truncation concentrates in low rungs.

total_games_and_sets.existing_mechanism: Totals derive from the full match distribution: the rating gap (closeness) controls whether it goes the distance, hold probabilities control games per set and tiebreaks, format caps length, and retirement truncates totals. The rung ladder must be consistent with the match-winner and set-spread markets.
total_games_and_sets.label: Total games and total sets

existing_interactions.hypothesis: Early long matches reduce later rounds; path dependence.
Uncertainty flattens favourites.
Withdrawals reshuffle bracket slots.

tournament_winner_futures.existing_mechanism: Futures are a path product of match-win probabilities across a specific bracket, with fatigue accumulation, seeding, withdrawals and correlation within halves. Before the draw, probabilities average over draw randomness. Rating uncertainty flattens favourites, and retirement/walkover rules affect advancement.
